14133-david-balfour-being-memoirs-of-his:
Robert Louis Stevenson's David Balfour continues the hero's story after Kidnapped, now tangled in the Appin murder case. David faces Lord Advocate Grant, suffers captivity on the Bass Rock, and travels into Holland and France. James More Drummond, son of Rob Roy, and his daughter Catriona shape the second half, with loyalty, law, and love pulling David in turn.

Stevenson warns in his dedication that sequels disappoint, then proves himself wrong. Scots speech, sea cabins, and courtroom pressure give the tale texture, while Catriona's plea for David's life on her knees forms its emotional peak. Six passengers share a cabin on one voyage, merchants from Leith, Kirkcaldy, and Dundee among them. Adventure and feeling balance here, and the novel closes David's youth with honor intact and affection earned.
21337-that-very-mab:
May Kendall and Andrew Lang wrote this satirical fantasy together, published in London in 1885, in which Queen Mab returns to modern earth. Moonlight floods a sacred island in Samoa as her voice rises from the Calling Place and the sea itself shudders. From the Pacific she comes to inspect Victorian England.

Chapters send Mab through disillusions. She meets debates on the origin of religion, a poet facing a palaeontologist of theology, machinery, the successful merchant, and justice under the new democracy. A nihilist, a democrat, and a professor offer suggestions to a bishop. The result is a light, sharp fable using fairy machinery to mock the science, politics, and sermons of 1885.
4223-the-mystery-of-a-hansom-cab:
Fergus Hume's Mystery of a Hansom Cab, the best-selling Melbourne detective tale, opens its eighth chapter with Brian taking a walk and a drive. In a drawing room, a young lady plays a detestable morceau de salon, variations embroidering an air till the tune is an agony to find.

The melody is Over the Garden Wall, with variations by Signor Thump, a comic touch in a murder mystery. Hume builds his plot from cab rides, society parties, and a dead man found in a cab. Readers who enjoy Victorian sensation fiction will find a fast, atmospheric puzzle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-achab:
Achab, son of Amri and King of Israel, reigned 918 to 897 BC by 1 Kings 16:29, though Assyrian documents give 875 to 854, and the original reading may have changed. Married to Jezabel, a Sidonian princess, he was misled by her into idolatry, persecution of the prophets, and grievous injustice against Naboth. He twice defeated Syria in war, then allied with the Syrian king Benadad despite prophetic warning.

In Salmanassar II's sixth year the allies were beaten near Karkar by the Assyrians, ending their compact. Achab then allied with Josaphat of Juda to conquer Ramoth Galaad. False prophets promised victory; Micheas predicted defeat. An arrow wounded Achab between lungs and stomach, he died that evening, and dogs licked his blood where his chariot was washed in Samaria's pool.

doe-osti-3677342-final-technical-report-: When hurricanes knock out the grid, the poorest neighborhoods wait longest for power. The REDDI Communities final report covers resilient renewable energy projects that shrink disaster impact. Solar-plus-storage systems keep clinics, shelters, and homes running when the grid fails.
nasa-tm-19650014229-some-design-consider:
Robert H Johns, Reeves P Cochran, and David A Spera at Lewis Research Center wrote this report on spinning satellites with expandable structures. Some spacecraft need large flat areas, for radiators, solar collectors, or dust-catching experiments. Those areas must unfold or expand after launch, since a rocket nose cone is small.

Spinning keeps such a satellite steady, but it also stresses the expanded parts. The authors weigh design choices for that combination. They look at rigid expandable structures, which hold their shape once opened. The problem is a balance: enough area for the job, enough strength to survive spin, and a package small enough to launch.
nasa-tm-19690010288-a-systems-analysis-o:
A systems analysis of a regenerative cabin atmosphere control system forms this master's thesis in mechanical engineering. It comes from the University of Virginia's School of Engineering and Applied Science. Regenerative systems recycle cabin air for long missions instead of storing all breathing gases at launch. The thesis first models a space cabin, its crew, and its atmosphere.

Long chapters then describe each component in turn. They include blowers and ducting, water separators, bypass dampers, and a carbon dioxide concentrator. A reduction unit and an electrolysis unit follow, with nitrogen control and pressure sensors after them. System block diagrams then tie the parts together. The whole forms an engineering blueprint for keeping cabin air breathable on long flights.
the-mystery-of-a-hansom-cab:
Fergus Hume's detective novel The Mystery of a Hansom Cab is present here only through a full contents list. A bare heading, Preface, follows it. Neither the preface text nor the story appears. Thirty-five chapters are listed. What the Argus Said opens the book, and The Evidence at the Inquest follows, with a hundred pounds reward offered in Chapter III.

A detective named Gorby makes a start and further discoveries, while another investigator, Kilsip, later forms a theory of his own. The Trial, The Verdict of the Jury, and Sal Rawlins Tells All She Knows fill the middle list. Hush-Money, The Confession, and The Hands of Justice close the visible contents near the end.
